t: Greek tyrants were men who seized sole power in a city-state outside its traditional order, often by championing the common people against a narrow aristocracy.
Some, such as Cypselus of Corinth and Peisistratus of Athens, presided over prosperity, public building and new festivals, but few tyrannies outlasted the founder’s sons.
Plato and Aristotle made the tyrant the type of the worst ruler, governing for himself and without law, and their judgement fixed the meaning the word has had ever since.
dyk: Herodotus tells that Peisistratus regained Athens after his first exile by entering the city in a chariot beside a tall woman named Phye, dressed in armour as Athena, while heralds proclaimed that the goddess was bringing him home.
ev: Cypselus overthrows the Bacchiad aristocracy and makes himself tyrant of Corinth (traditional date)
Peisistratus defeats the Athenians at Pallene and begins his third and longest tyranny
Harmodius and Aristogeiton kill Hipparchus; Sparta drives out his brother Hippias in 510 BCE
Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Acragas defeat a Carthaginian army at Himera
Dionysius I seizes power in Syracuse during a war with Carthage and rules until 367 BCE
Sparta installs the Thirty Tyrants, an oligarchy that rules Athens by terror until 403 BCE
Nabis, the last independent ruler of Sparta, is assassinated and Sparta is forced into the Achaean League
Rome destroys Corinth and brings the cities of southern Greece under Roman control

f.power: A single ruler, the tyrannos, backed by a bodyguard or mercenaries, with relatives and allies in the main offices and the city’s laws and magistracies often left in place
f.legitimacy: None by law or ancestral right: power won by force, fraud or popular support against the ruling aristocrats, and kept by results, patronage, religious display and fear
f.chosen: Seized by coup, often with popular or mercenary backing; usually passed to sons but seldom beyond them; ended by assassination, revolt or the intervention of Sparta and other powers
f.examples: Corinth under the Cypselids, Sicyon under the Orthagorids, Athens under the Peisistratids (546–510 BCE), Samos under Polycrates, Syracuse under Dionysius I (405–367 BCE)
